summary: Arabic is a Semitic language of the Afro-Asiatic family, the closest relative of Hebrew in this course. You learn Modern Standard Arabic (الْفُصْحَى), the written and formal language shared by the whole Arab world; at home people speak regional dialects. It is written from right to left with 28 letters for consonants and long vowels — the short vowels are small optional marks — and most words are built from roots of three consonants.

facts.label: Family
facts.value: Afro-Asiatic › Semitic › Central Semitic — with Hebrew and Aramaic as close relatives

facts.label: Script and direction
facts.value: Arabic script, right to left; 28 letters that join and change shape; short vowels are marks above or below the letters and are usually left out; numbers run left to right

facts.label: Standard variety
facts.value: Modern Standard Arabic (الْفُصْحَى) for writing, news and formal speech; everyday speech in dialects (Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf, Iraqi, Maghrebi …) — two layers side by side, called diglossia

facts.label: Where
facts.value: official language of more than 20 countries from Morocco to Iraq and Oman; one of the six official languages of the United Nations; the language of the Qurʾān

facts.label: Speakers
facts.value: more than 300 million native speakers of Arabic dialects; Standard Arabic is learned at school

typology.why: Arabic weaves a root of consonants into a pattern of vowels inside the word (k-t-b “writing” → كَتَبَ kataba “he wrote”, كِتَاب kitāb “book”, كَاتِب kātib “writer”), and one ending carries several meanings at once: the -at of كَتَبَتْ says 3rd person + singular + feminine + past together.
typology.alsoShows: Agglutinating touches: small words are attached in front — وَ “and”, الْ “the”, بِـ “with” — and pronoun endings behind (كِتَابِي “my book”), each piece with one meaning.

peculiarities.title: Right to left, letters joined
peculiarities.text: Words run from right to left and the letters connect, taking up to four shapes; six letters (ا د ذ ر ز و) never join the letter after them.

peculiarities.title: Short vowels are not written
peculiarities.text: Normal texts show only consonants and long vowels: كتب can be كَتَبَ (he wrote), كُتُبٌ (books) or كُتِبَ (it was written). This course shows every vowel mark until you can read without them.

peculiarities.title: Roots and patterns
peculiarities.text: Three consonants carry a meaning and patterns make words of it: ك ت ب → كِتَاب book, مَكْتَب desk, office, كَاتِب writer, مَكْتَبَة library. Learn the patterns and you can guess new words.

peculiarities.title: No “to be” in the present
peculiarities.text: أَنَا طَالِبٌ = “I (am) a student”: subject and predicate simply stand side by side. The verb كَانَ appears only in the past and future: كُنْتُ طَالِبًا, I was a student.

peculiarities.title: Two genders — even for “you”
peculiarities.text: Every noun is masculine or feminine (most feminines end in ة). “You” is أَنْتَ to a man and أَنْتِ to a woman, and greetings change with it: كَيْفَ حَالُكَ / كَيْفَ حَالُكِ.

peculiarities.title: Singular, dual, plural — and broken plurals
peculiarities.text: Two of anything have their own form, the dual. Many plurals change the inside of the word: كِتَاب → كُتُب, رَجُل → رِجَال. Learn every noun with its plural.

peculiarities.title: The definite article is a prefix, the indefinite an ending
peculiarities.text: بَيْتٌ (baytun) = a house, الْبَيْتُ (al-baytu) = the house. Before “sun letters” the l of al- is not heard: الشَّقَّةُ = aš-šaqqa.

peculiarities.title: Things in the plural are “she”
peculiarities.text: Plurals of things take feminine singular agreement: هٰذِهِ الْكُتُبُ (these books), الْكُتُبُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا (the books? they are here).

pathNote: Arabic walks the fusional path: the same 19 steps and the same words as Hebrew, Chinese and German, with the grammar of a fusional, root-and-pattern language at each step. S00 the overview: an abjad written right to left, roots and patterns, Modern Standard Arabic and the dialects. S01 subject pronouns with gender (أَنْتَ / أَنْتِ, هُمْ / هُنَّ) and the verbless present “to be” (أَنَا طَالِبٌ), with كَانَ for the past. S02 greetings with fixed answers that change with the listener (كَيْفَ حَالُكَ / حَالُكِ). S03 demonstratives that agree (هٰذَا / هٰذِهِ / هٰؤُلَاءِ, ذٰلِكَ / تِلْكَ / أُولٰئِكَ). S04 gender, al- and tanwīn, agreement (things in the plural are feminine singular) and the cases, starting with the nominative. S05 numbers with the dual, broken plurals and the reversed gender of 3–10. S06 “to have” with عِنْدَ and the possessive endings (كِتَابِي). S07 the present conjugation (prefixes and endings), the accusative object, and roots and patterns. S08 a negator chosen by the kind of sentence and the tense (لَا، لَيْسَ، لَمْ، لَنْ). S09 yes/no questions with هَلْ and أَ, and بَلَى. S10 question words at the front (مَاذَا / مَا, مَنْ, أَيْنَ …). S11 prepositions with the genitive, and the attached بِـ and لِـ. S12 place words that are old accusative nouns (أَمَامَ, خَلْفَ) and the adjectives قَرِيبٌ مِنْ / بَعِيدٌ عَنْ. S13 verbs of movement — hollow and weak verbs — and the imperative with four forms (اِذْهَبْ، اِذْهَبِي، اِذْهَبُوا، اِذْهَبْنَ). S14 the adverbial accusative of time (يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ, صَبَاحًا). S15 the time prepositions, the hour with feminine ordinals, and two sets of month names. S16 adjectives after the noun, agreeing in gender, number, case and definiteness, with broken plurals for people. S17 the elative أَفْعَل (أَكْبَرُ مِنْ, الْأَكْبَرُ) and the colours أَفْعَل / فَعْلَاء / فُعْل. S18 linking words: لِأَنَّ / أَنَّ / لٰكِنَّ / مَعَ أَنَّ with an accusative or a pronoun ending, أَنْ with the subjunctive, إِذَا with the past and فَـ. The isolating path (Chinese) spends these steps on tones, measure words, word order and aspect particles; the agglutinating path on suffix chains and vowel harmony.

quiz.why: Roots are woven into vowel patterns inside the word, and one ending carries several meanings at once.

quiz.q: How do you say “I am a student” (a man speaking)?
quiz.why: The present of “to be” is not said: subject + predicate.

quiz.q: In which direction is Arabic written?
quiz.why: Words run right to left; only numbers run left to right.

quiz.q: What do كِتَاب, كَاتِب and مَكْتَب have in common?
quiz.why: Book, writer, office: one root, different patterns.
أَنْتَ (-ta) to a man, أَنْتِ (-ti) to a woman, أَنْتُمْ to several people.
The ending -un (tanwīn) marks an indefinite noun; “the house” is الْبَيْتُ.

quiz.q: Which variety does this course teach?
quiz.why: MSA is the shared written and formal language; dialects differ by region.

notes.text:
Hundreds of Portuguese words come from Arabic, many with the article al- fused in:
→ azeite (الزَّيْت), arroz (الرُّزّ), açúcar (السُّكَّر), aldeia (الضَّيْعَة), alface (الْخَسّ), oxalá (لَوْ شَاءَ اللّٰهُ)

Familiar: two genders, agreement, adjectives after the noun, a dropped subject pronoun, and one simple past for a finished action (comi = أَكَلْتُ).

New:
- three cases, the dual, “you” by gender;
- no “to be” in the present (so no ser / estar choice);
- only three vowel qualities.

If your language is fusional, much is familiar: endings that pack case, number and gender, agreement, and a fairly free word order.

New:
- roots of three consonants that change inside the word (كِتَاب → كُتُب);
- the article as a prefix.

If your language is agglutinating, some Arabic pieces will feel familiar — وَ, الْ, بِـ joined in front, pronoun endings behind (كِتَابِي).

But **the core is fusional and root-and-pattern**:
→ كَتَبَ, كِتَاب, كُتُب, مَكْتَب share only k-t-b
